quests.title: The Toll That Was Not Taken

giver.location: Gideon, the counting floor above the toll gate

quests.directions: Belliene keeps the counting floor over the toll gate, at the river end of the Gideon market cross. The barge she wants looked at ties up at the third mooring below the gate, past the timber yard, on the side where the willows come down to the water. Go before the second bell or the crew will be ashore.

journal.text: A porter on the Gideon quay said the Ledger has been weighing the same barge twice and writing it down once. He would not say it twice.
Factor Belliene wants me to find out who is taking a cut off the river tolls. She says it is costing the Ledger nine hundred a season and that she has been told to be discreet about it.

The barge at the third mooring is the Wren, out of Soulrest, and her master is a Breton called Anse. The tally chalked on her rail does not match the tally in the gate book. The gate book is in Belliene's own hand.
Anse says he pays what he is asked and gets a chit for it. He showed me the chits. There are two kinds, and one kind has no seal on it at all.

The unsealed chits go back four seasons and they are all in the same hand as the gate book. Belliene has not lost nine hundred a season. She has taken it, and she has sent me to find someone to have taken it.
Wuleen-Kus in the low market says the Ledger has done this before, in Lilmoth, and that the man they hung it on was a Naga porter who could not read the book he was supposed to have written in.
Anse cast off in the night and took the chits with him. Whatever they proved, they prove it somewhere down the coast now.
Anse is dead in his own hold and the chits went into the river with the rest of his papers. Belliene has stopped asking me about the tolls.
I gave Belliene a name and it was not hers. The porter has been put off the quay and will not work the river again. She paid me and told me I have a head for this work.
I laid the unsealed chits in front of the Ledger's own assembly with Anse standing beside me. Belliene did not deny it. She was quiet, which was worse, and then she named two others.
I told Belliene what I had and what it would cost her to have it. She pays me a share now. I am in the ledger she keeps for the things that are not in the ledger.
I gave the chits to Anse and told him to take them out of the province. He asked what I wanted for them. I said nothing, and he did not believe me, and he went anyway.
Belliene keeps a second set of weights in the locked press under the window. I took one stone of it. One stone is a whole argument.

branches.condition: The player has the unsealed chits in hand and can read whose writing is on them
The player knows Belliene wrote the book she is complaining about, and must decide who is owed it

resolutions.outcome: A porter who cannot read is put off the quay for a theft Belliene committed. The Ledger's books are closed and the tolls go on being taken twice.
The unsealed chits are read into the Ledger's assembly. Belliene is stripped of the toll gate and names two others on her way out; the gate passes to a factor who does not like outlanders.
Belliene keeps the gate and the player keeps a share. The theft continues, quieter, with two people in it. The Dockhands go on being short.
resolutions.attribute_scale_note: W1-ATTR-SCALE. Was `personality: 40`. W1-ATTR-SCALE. Re-set from the MEASURED ceiling with reserve, not clamped to it. Attributes are earned only at +1 per multiple of 15 crossed in a governing skill (character/derive.js:359); the bought stream exists in engine.js _spendSouls() and is unfundable, because nothing in the build awards souls. So an attribute is worth `creation + 6 per governing skill` and no more, measured over 240 signatures in reports/faction-signature-sweep.json. The new value sits at or under `median ceiling - 2`; clamping to the ceiling itself is the zero-margin defect that shut Act IV for 11 of 40 signatures one point lower. Checked by tools/quests/attr-scale-audit.mjs.

resolutions.outcome: The chits leave the province with the only man who was ever going to be believed holding them. Nothing is proved, nothing is punished, and the Wren does not put in at Gideon again.
Belliene keeps two sets of weights, and the second set is in the locked press under the window. You take one stone of it. One stone is a whole argument.

failure_states.cause: Six days pass after journal index 20 without the player reading the chits
failure_states.consequence: The Wren sails. Only res_scapegoat remains reachable and Belliene's account becomes the only account.
The chits are lost with him; the quest closes unresolved and the Dockhands lose eleven gold a week for good.

deceit.stated_objective: Find whoever is stealing from the river tolls
deceit.actual_objective: Have somebody else found to have stolen from the river tolls
deceit.truth: Belliene has been writing the gate book short for four seasons and pocketing the difference.

rewards.name: a share of the short weight

quests.notes: W1-18. Four exclusive endings, none of which requires violence. The deceit is D1/D2/D8: the giver's stated loss is her own theft, and the pattern repeats a real earlier crime the player can hear about from a rival.

quests.title: Eleven Gold a Week

giver.location: Gideon, the shelter at the foot of the crane

quests.directions: The porters shelter under the crane at the downstream end of the Gideon quay, where the cobbles give out. Eeja is the one with the strapping on both hands. The Ledger's pay clerk works out of the shed behind the timber stack, up the plank ramp.

journal.text: Eeja says the porters have been paid eleven gold a week short since Rain's Hand and that the shortfall has no name on it. She is not asking me to fix it. She is asking me to count.
I counted. Forty-one porters, and the pay shed's book says thirty. The eleven who are not in the book are all Naga, and all of them work.
The pay clerk says the eleven were never taken on, that they turn up and carry and get paid out of the shortfall by the other thirty. He says this as though it explains something.
It is not theft. It is that eleven people are not written down anywhere, and so they need not be paid. Eeja knew that before she asked me to count. She wanted a person who could read to have seen it.
The eleven were put off the quay before I got the count to anyone. Not a man at the pay shed remembers their names, including me.

The eleven are in the book. The Ledger's clerk wrote them in himself and the thirty are paid the same as before, and the quay is a little poorer and a little quieter, and Eeja shook my hand for a long time.

The porters stopped working and the barges sat for four days. They are in the book now. Two of them are not, because they were taken by the Legion on the second day, and I cannot get an answer as to where.
I took the count to the Assize instead. The clerk was fined and the eleven were sent back to Soulrest as unlicensed labour, which is the law, and which is not what I meant.
I got into the dock office at the change of shift and copied the roll by the light off the water. Eleven gold a week, in the harbourmaster's own hand, for men he swore he never hired.

branches.condition: The count is done and the player must decide who is shown it
The player can write the eleven names down or leave them unwritten

resolutions.outcome: The eleven are entered in the pay book. The Ledger absorbs the cost by cutting the timber gang, which nobody mentions to the timber gang.
Four days of stopped barges force the entry. Two of the eleven are taken by the Legion during the stoppage and do not come back; the quay wins and is short by two.
The Assize fines the clerk and deports the eleven as unlicensed labour. The law is satisfied and the quay is eleven people emptier.
You get into the dock office at the change of shift and copy the roll by the light coming off the water. Eleven gold a week, in the harbourmaster's own hand, for men he swore he had never hired.

failure_states.cause: The player completes Q-LEDG-01 through res_scapegoat before finishing the count
failure_states.consequence: The unwritten eleven are cleared off the quay with the scapegoat. The quest closes and the Dockhands never open to the player.

quests.notes: W1-18. A quest with no villain and no combat resolution at all. Its failure state is caused by another quest's ending, which is the cross-quest coupling RI-QST09 K2 counts.

quests.title: What the Cutting Leaves

giver.location: the hollow, a day east of Helstrom on the root track

quests.directions: Leave Helstrom by the eastern sapwell and follow the root track until the roots start to show knife-work. Where the cutting stops you are inside Deep-Kin ground and they will know it before you do. The cut sapwell itself is a half-morning further, downhill, where the water lies still and yellow.

journal.text: Teel-Ashaan says a sapwell east of the hollow has been cut and asks me to see it and come back and say what I saw. He did not tell me what to look for. I think that was on purpose.
The well has been cut four times, in four seasons, always the same depth and always on the shaded side. Whoever did it knew what they were doing and did not want the tree to die.
There are three phial-stoppers in the mud and a boot print that is not a boot. A drinker was here as well as a cutter.

The cutter is Deep-Kin. The stoppers are Ixtu-Vakh work but the knife-hand is one of Teel-Ashaan's own, and the tree is still standing because whoever cut it loves it. That is worse for them, not better.
Ashaan-Hulei says she cuts it because the hollow has nothing else to trade and because the tree has not objected. She asked me whether I had ever asked a tree anything.
The well was cut through while I was still deciding, and this time it was not careful. There is nothing left to bring anyone to see.
I told Teel-Ashaan whose knife it was. Ashaan-Hulei has been put out of the hollow and the sapwell is watched. The Deep-Kin trust me and are quieter around me than they were.
I said the cutting was Ixtu-Vakh and let the stoppers say the rest. It is true in the way a thing can be true and wrong. Ashaan-Hulei knows what I did and has not said so.

I brought the two of them to the well together and made them stand in front of it. They argued for an hour and then agreed a depth and a season. Neither of them thanked me and both look at me differently now.
I followed the cutters out to the stand and lay in the mud a hundred paces off while they worked. What the cutting leaves, I watched them leave it.

branches.condition: The player can read the cut and the stoppers, or take the well at face value
The player knows the cutter is Deep-Kin and must decide who is told

resolutions.outcome: Ashaan-Hulei is put out of the hollow and the well is watched. The Deep-Kin close the eastern root track to outsiders, which shortens the road to Helstrom for nobody.
The Ixtu-Vakh are blamed for a cutting they did not make. Two of their runners are killed on the root track within the month and the Deep-Kin stop selling them anything at all.
A depth and a season are agreed in front of the well. The cutting continues, legally, at a rate the tree survives, and both factions distrust the player exactly as much as each other.
You follow the cutters out to the stand and lie in the mud a hundred paces off while they work. What the cutting leaves, you see them leave it.

failure_states.cause: Twelve days pass after journal index 20 with no resolution
failure_states.consequence: The well is cut through. The Deep-Kin close the hollow to the player; every Xul-Aneekh quest above rank 2 becomes unreachable in this save.

deceit.stated_objective: See the cut sapwell and report what is there
deceit.actual_objective: See the cut sapwell and report what is there
deceit.truth: Teel-Ashaan already suspects one of his own and wants an outsider's mouth to say it.

quests.notes: W1-18. The giver is honest about the task and dishonest about the reason, which is D6/D11 rather than D1. Every ending closes a different questline; none requires a kill, though one causes two.
